description:
640 tiles at 16x16. A desert kingdom you can actually build: a mudbrick town wall with a horseshoe gate in it, a great sandstone court behind, flat whitewashed roofs with the things that stand on them, a panel of cobalt glazed tilework set into the paving, a walled basin with a fountain at its head, and the open oasis and date grove out past the wall.

Most desert packs give you dunes. This one gives you the architecture that stands on them — and the boundaries where each material meets every other one.

What is in the download

  • 517 of the 640 tiles are transitions — 81% of the pack. 11 complete 47-mask autotile sets, every inner corner, outer corner, edge, junction and single. Completeness is checked mechanically on every build rather than counted by hand, because a 47-mask set missing three tiles is broken in your map and you find out while you are painting.
  • 7 materials on a measured value ladder. A desert is the hardest subject in this series to keep readable, because sand, sandstone, mudbrick and plaster all want to sit at the top of the range together. No two materials here share more than one of {value, hue, structure}, and the smallest gap on the ladder is 22.6 luma — measured from the emitted pixels, not from a design document.
  • 22 objects across 62 tiles, each shipped twice on purpose: transparent, so you can drop it on your own ground, and grounded on each of our surfaces it belongs to with the contact shadow already drawn. 2 of them are flat paint and carry no shadow at all, because a shadow under a scatter of pebbles would make it hover.
  • 33 animation frames — 5 animated things: a fountain, a pierced hanging lamp, and 3 variants of the oasis surface. The water is declared as a ping-pong, so it breathes instead of lurching.
  • A finished sample map, 36x26 cells, shipped three ways: as a PNG, as a .tmx that opens in Tiled as a real map, and as JSON that names every cell by tile id so it rebuilds in any engine.
  • 37 4x4 proof renders, one per repeating tile, so you can look for the grid line yourself with the download open.
  • Every tile also as a loose PNG, and the same art as packed sheets. 764 files in total.

The importers were actually run

An importer is a claim about a program we do not run. So each of these was loaded by the engine it targets and made to count what it built:

  • RPG Maker MZ — an A2 autotile sheet, the page MZ's own autotile brush paints, plus B/C/D object pages and a slot map. Composed back out of the emitted sheet using MZ's own FLOOR_AUTOTILE_TABLE: 11 of 11 sets, 517 of 517 masked tiles, and 528 of 528 shapes came back byte-identical.
  • Tiled — one .tsx per group. All 15 were opened and rendered by Tiled's own tmxrasterizer and compared pixel for pixel against the shipped sheets: 752 tiles rendered, 0 differing.
  • Godot 4 — a .tres TileSet, loaded in Godot 4.7.2 and made to count: 15 atlas sources, 640 of 640 declared tiles built, and every multi-cell footprint exact. It was then installed the way you would actually install it — in a subfolder of a blank project, with a decoy file of the same name at the project root — and it resolved its own sheets, kept every tile, and painted onto a TileMapLayer.

What is proven, and what is not

The grid is exact, the palette is locked to 86 colours, the alpha is strictly binary with no anti-aliasing, every tile carries a declared role, and every autotile set is complete. Those are exact checks and they run on every build.

Seamlessness is not on that list, and we will not claim it. Every tile's wrap boundary is measured against its own interior, and every 4x4 repetition is rendered and reviewed — but that test is a measured floor rather than a proof, so the renders ship with the pack and you can judge them yourself. A weaker true claim beats a strong false one.

The autotile sets

  • oasis_on_dust — organic edge
  • oasis_on_sandstone — hard edge
  • grove_on_dust — organic edge
  • dust_on_sandstone — organic edge
  • sandstone_on_dust — hard edge
  • glaze_on_sandstone — hard edge
  • glaze_on_plaster — hard edge
  • mudbrick_on_dust — hard edge, with a wall face
  • mudbrick_on_sandstone — hard edge, with a wall face
  • plaster_on_dust — hard edge, with a wall face
  • plaster_on_sandstone — hard edge, with a wall face

It fits the rest of the series

This is Verdant 24. Every pack in the series is drawn from one palette, so a boundary between this pack's dust and another pack's grass is a boundary you can actually paint.
